cases.description: A scoped grant verified against the issuer key, for the named audience, inside its window, verifies.
The vendor-neutral network.ink.authorization_grant spelling is signed and verifies like the legacy spelling.
A grant presented at exactly issuedAt is inside the window (inclusive lower bound).
A grant that requires a verified owner verifies when the service supplies a verified owner status.
A grant that does not require a verified owner verifies even when the service supplies an unverified owner status; the hook is consulted only when the grant asks for it.
A different issuer's seen and revoked entry for the same grantId string does not block this grant; replay and revocation key on the (issuer, grantId) pair.
A grant with a broadened scope (bad signature) presented to the wrong audience still rejects on the signature, pinning signature-first ordering ahead of the audience check.
A grant with a broadened scope presented after expiry still rejects on the signature, not on expiry.
A grant with a broadened scope whose (issuer, grantId) is already seen still rejects on the signature, not on replay.
A grant with a broadened scope whose (issuer, grantId) is revoked still rejects on the signature, not on revocation.
An owner-requiring grant with a broadened scope and an unverified owner still rejects on the signature, not on owner verification.
Verifying against a different public key fails the signature check.
Broadening the scope after signing invalidates the signature.
Changing the subject after signing invalidates the signature.
A grant minted for did:web:service.example presented to a different service is rejected on the audience check even though the signature is valid.
Relabeling the grant audience to match the checking service after signing does not help: the signature bound the original audience.
A grant presented by the authenticated principal named as its subject verifies; the presentation binding holds.
A grant with no presenter supplied is a bearer artifact inside its window; the binding check is skipped.

An empty-string presenter means no presenter was established, so the binding check is skipped just as when it is absent; Go cannot tell an unset field from an empty one, so an empty presenter is no presenter across implementations.
A grant presented by a principal other than its signed subject is rejected on the presentation binding, so a stolen grant is not presentable by another principal.
A grant presented after expiresAt is rejected.
A grant presented at exactly expiresAt is rejected (exclusive upper bound).
A grant presented before issuedAt is rejected; issuer and verifier clock skew must not admit a future grant.
A grant whose (issuer, grantId) is already in the service's seen set is a replay and is rejected.
A grant whose (issuer, grantId) is on the service's revocation list is rejected even inside the window.
A grant that requires a verified owner is rejected when the owner status is unverified.
A grant that requires a verified owner is rejected when the service supplies no owner status; absent is not verified.
An unknown top-level field is rejected by the strict schema before verification.
A lone UTF-16 surrogate in a string field is not portable and rejects structurally as schema, before the signature.
A grant with no scope entries is out of profile and rejects.
A grant with a repeated scope entry is rejected; scope entries must be distinct so two implementations count the same set.
A scope array with more than 64 entries is out of profile and rejects.
A scope array with a non-string entry rejects.
A scope entry longer than 128 code units is out of profile and rejects.
An issuer longer than 512 code units is out of profile and rejects.
A subject longer than 512 code units is out of profile and rejects.
An audience longer than 512 code units is out of profile and rejects.
A grantId longer than 256 code units is out of profile and rejects.
A protocol other than ink/0.1 is out of profile and rejects.
A type that is neither the network.tulpa nor the network.ink spelling is out of profile and rejects.
A grant whose expiresAt is not after issuedAt is malformed and rejects.
A grant whose window exceeds the ten-minute maximum lifetime is out of profile and rejects structurally, before the signature, even against a wrong key.
A grant inside the profile window but longer than a caller-tightened maxLifetimeMs is rejected as schema, after the signature.

A caller-tightened maxLifetimeMs of exactly 0 means unset and uses the profile default, so a grant inside the profile window still verifies; Go cannot tell a zero-value integer from an unset one, so 0 is no caller cap across implementations.
A negative caller-tightened maxLifetimeMs is a verifier input error that fails closed as schema, not a policy that admits every window, after the signature.
A grant whose issuedAt is not a strict INK timestamp rejects.
A signature that is not valid base64url of the right length is rejected.
A grant with no signature field rejects.
A grantId shorter than 16 code units is out of profile and rejects.
A verifier clock that is not a strict INK timestamp is a verifier input error and fails closed as schema, not a window verdict.
The same signed grant presented as raw wire text verifies: whitespace between tokens is legal JSON and vanishes at canonicalization, so the signature still covers it.

An out-of-range number literal shadowed by a later duplicate member rejects. Member semantics are last-wins, so the literal never reaches the parsed grant and the signature over the canonical form still verifies; only a gate on the raw text sees it, and without one two implementations admit different byte strings for the same signed grant.
An out-of-range number literal in a live member rejects at the raw gate, before the schema can rule on the Infinity a lenient parser would hand it.
An underflowing exponent is in range: every IEEE-754 parser decodes 1e-400 to 0, so a shadowed one is not gated and the grant behind it verifies. The gate is a range test, not a ban on exponents.
A lone UTF-16 surrogate escape in the raw text rejects structurally, before the signature: a parser that rewrites it to U+FFFD would canonicalize something other than what was sent.
